URL: https://cnn.com/2026/10/26/europe/un-report-russia-ukraine-intl
(CNN, 26 Oct)

Russian forces have been targeting Ukrainian power infrastructure since the early months of the war in 2022, and massively ramped up these attacks at the beginning of last year’s winter, leaving millions of Ukrainians freezing in the darkness of their homes.

A new report published by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine on Monday and shared with CNN, said these attacks “were carried out with intent” and were in line with Russia’s “state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering.”

“Russian commanders who were ordering these attacks knew that the heating facilities they targeted were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter,” the report, which is being submitted to the UN General Assembly, said.

CNN has approached the Kremlin for comment.

Polish volunteers cook soup in a Kyiv neighborhood left without electricity and heating following Russian attacks during freezing temperatures in February 2026.
    
  
          Thomas Peter/Reuters/File
        
      
    
    


    
            Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the report “confirms what Ukrainians have experienced for years: Russia’s systematic attacks on civilian energy infrastructure constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

In a post on X, Sybiha said Russia “has deliberately deprived millions of people of electricity, heating and water, turning cold and darkness into instruments of war.”

In a statement released on Monday, the Russian Permanent Mission – the official delegation that represents Russia to the UN – rejected the commission’s findings, claiming it had drawn on “falsified” data and alleging it was set up by a “politicized body.”

“Russia does not recognize the mandate of this commission, which was established through a resolution passed by a politicized body – the UN Human Rights Council,” the delegation said.

“The commission bases its findings on falsified data provided by the Ukrainian authorities via the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) presence in Kyiv,” it added.

The Russian Permanent Mission claimed the UN Human Rights Council “simply fails to notice any crimes committed by the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”

Large-scale Russian drone and missile attacks last winter reduced Ukraine’s thermal power generation capacities by 70 per cent in the most affected areas, according to Kyiv. The suffering was made worse by an unusually cold winter with temperatures dropping to as low as -30 degrees Celsius (-22 F) on multiple occasions.

The commission was established by the UN’s Human Rights Council just days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

It has previously reported on other aspects of Russia’s war on Ukraine, including allegations of sexual and gender-based violence committed by Russian armed forces, and the wide-spread forced deportations of Ukrainian children by Russian authorities.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, following an interview in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. "Now, we have dangerous days ahead of the elections," Zelenskyy said on Sunday, referring to the Nov. 3 midterms in the US. Photographer: Olga Ivashchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images
    
  
          Olga Ivashchenko/Bloomberg/Getty Images
        
      
    
    


    
    
      
        Nothing personal between me and Trump, Zelensky tells CNN

In this latest report, the commission describes the dire impacts of prolonged cold exposure on Ukrainian civilians, saying that the country’s medical authorities documented deaths caused by low temperatures in homes, and even in hospitals.

“Medical personnel from hospitals reported that during the past winter, they attended to patients who developed cold-related trauma, including various degrees of frostbite and hypothermia. The patients had developed these conditions at home, due to exposure to unheated premises and required hospitalization,” the report said.

The report quotes a civilian woman living in Dnipro, Ukraine’s fourth largest city, who describes the impact the Russian attacks had on her. “Cold—it paralyzes you; there’s simply no way to get warm, and terrifying thoughts come into your mind,” she said.

Electricians work to restore the power grid in front of a destroyed private house in Kyiv region. A a 14-year-old was killed in the attack on September 30.
    
  
          Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP/Getty Images
        
      
    
    


    
            Blaming Putin and others

The UN commission report names several high-profile Russian officials as the people most responsible for what it describes as “war crimes and the crimes against humanity.”

It says Russian President Vladimir Putin made several “statements concerning instructions to commit attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.”

It also alleges that evidence collected over the past few years shows that Russia’s former Minister of Defence Sergei Shoigu and his successor Andrey Belousov, as well the Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, have been responsible for planning and overseeing attacks.

The International Criminal Court has previously issued arrest warrants against Putin, Shoigu and Gerasimov for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

In this still taken from video posted to the social media platform Telegram, a Russian drone strikes Masha Yivzhenko's workplace in Kyiv on September 25.
    
  
          From Telegram
        
      
    
    


    
    
      
        Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone

As the colder weather begins to arrive in Ukraine, Russia has made it clear it intends to continue to terrorize its neighbor.

On Monday night, Russian ballistic missiles hit the grounds of a university in Kyiv, and surrounding areas including near a metro station and residential buildings, Zelensky said in his nightly address. Rescue operations are underway amid reports of people trapped under the rubble, he added.

“The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby,” the Ukrainian president said. “This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure.”

The report mentions a declaration made by the Russian Ministry of Defence in August, which announced attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and said: “In winter you will freeze.”

Ukraine is increasingly struggling to defend itself against these large-scale attacks because of a critical shortage of air defense missiles. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has made repeated pleas with Kyiv’s western allies for more ammunition, specifically pointing to the upcoming winter as a major worry.

Kyiv had been targeting Russian oil and gas infrastructure, in efforts to hurt the Kremlin’s revenues from energy exports. However, it has eased these attacks after criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for rising gas prices.

The report released on Monday also investigated Russia’s methods of recruiting foreign nationals to serve in its armed forces, concluding they amount to human rights violations and trafficking.

CNN has reported extensively on Russia’s use of deception, bribery and blackmail to lure foreigners into joining its military. People from multiple countries in Africa, India and Latin America have described being promised jobs in Russia only to find themselves on the frontlines.

The commission said it found “compelling evidence” that Russian authorities, working with agents, have “trafficked persons from 29 countries, using deception or coercion, to recruit them in the Russian armed forces.”

It said the fact that Russia has used the same tactics to recruit people from multiple countries “demonstrates a high degree of coordination between agents operating around the world and the Russian authorities.“

“Promised payments and bonuses were usually diverted by recruiting agents and military commanders, passports and phones were often confiscated, and contacts between agents and families were interrupted, once the recruits were deployed to the front.”

The report concludes that Russia violated the recruits’ fundamental human rights, including the rights to life, freedom, health, and to be treated humanely.

The commission also investigated Ukraine’s recruitment of foreign nationals into its army and said that testimonies it collected showed that those joining the Ukrainian armed forces “did so knowingly and voluntarily,” understood the contracts they were signing and received salaries.
